clue.text: Grazing land beyond river in Yorkshire

parts.note: once you are beyond a point you are past it
the Ure runs down Wensleydale in North Yorkshire, and setters reach for it whenever they want three quiet letters

explanation.surface: Sheep country lying on the far side of a Yorkshire river.
explanation.walkthrough: British rivers are worth collecting — Ure, Exe, Cam, Dee — because a setter who needs two or three vowel-heavy letters will call on one of them every time.
explanation.definitionFit: PASTURE is the grass land that livestock are turned out onto to feed, which is exactly grazing land.

clue.text: Song about blokes in former Soviet state

indicators.note: Something written about a subject is wrapped round it, so the first word's letters open out and the second word sits in the gap.

parts.note: an aria is the big solo song in an opera
blokes is everyday British for men

explanation.surface: A tune going round about the lads, sung in a country once behind the Iron Curtain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is doing two jobs at once — what a song is about, and where one word goes relative to another — which is why the sentence never sounds like an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: ARMENIA was a republic of the USSR until 1991 and has been independent since, so 'former Soviet state' names it exactly.

clue.text: Perhaps Mr T wearing hat

indicators.note: You wear a hat on top of yourself, so the single letter ends up tucked inside the word for the headgear.

parts.note: a tile is old slang for a hat, the sort of word that survives mainly in crosswords
the letter is used exactly as printed

explanation.surface: Mr T of the A-Team in a piece of headgear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is doing the work of 'for example': Mr is not the answer but one instance of it, and that little word is the only warning you get.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr, Dr, Lady and Sir are all titles, so 'Perhaps Mr' defines by holding up a single example of the class.

clue.text: A cottager wanting company turned up for sporting event

indicators.note: A thing that is wanting is short of something, so whatever is named next is missing from the letters you assemble.
In a down entry the answer runs towards the bottom, so reading it up the column means reading the letters the other way round.

parts.note: the two words run together, all nine letters, before anything comes out
co is the standard abbreviation, the one on the end of a firm's name

explanation.surface: A lonely cottage-dweller showing up for a day's sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' reads as lonely in the sentence and as short of in the wordplay, which is the double duty that keeps the surface smooth enough to believe.
explanation.definitionFit: A REGATTA is a meeting of boat races held over a day or a week, so the definition names the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Set off bouncy character taking Ritalin, primarily

indicators.note: Somebody taking a pill has swallowed it, so the letter goes inside the longer word rather than beside it.

parts.note: the tiger in Winnie-the-Pooh who bounces everywhere on his tail

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of the word it marks is used.

parts.note: the first letter of the drug's name, and nothing else of it

explanation.surface: A hyperactive character being medicated to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: Tigger is the bounciest character in Winnie-the-Pooh, so the surface reads as somebody prescribing him something to settle him, and 'bouncy character' does not look like a name.
explanation.definitionFit: To TRIGGER something is to set it off, a sense borrowed straight from the part of a gun you pull to fire it.

clue.text: Change location of temporary relief, heartlessly

indicators.note: A word robbed of its heart loses the letter at its exact centre, which a seven-letter word has.

parts.note: a respite is a short break from something hard, and it is the letter at its dead centre that goes

explanation.surface: A brief let-up granted without a scrap of sympathy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartlessly' reads as cruelly in the sentence and as an instruction underneath, and the convention is worth owning: the heart of a word is its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To RESITE something is to take it down and put it up somewhere else, which is changing its location.

clue.text: Content to snog a ribald Italian revolutionary

indicators.note: Taken as a noun rather than an adjective, the content of something is what sits inside it, so a run of letters is already lying there.

parts.note: nine letters in a row, starting inside the first word and stopping one letter into the last

explanation.surface: Somebody quite happy to kiss a coarse-humoured Italian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' is the trap: it reads as the adjective, meaning willing, and the noun is what flags the hiding place. Nine buried letters are harder to spot than four, because nobody scans for a span that long.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Garibaldi led the red-shirted volunteers whose campaigns unified Italy in the 1860s, so 'revolutionary' names the trade.

clue.text: People who dodge adverse exercises

indicators.note: Exercising a body moves its parts about, so the letters put through the workout come out standing somewhere else.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, with two E's to keep count of

explanation.surface: A punishing set of drills that nobody is enjoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adverse exercises' reads as one ordinary phrase — hard training — which is exactly why neither word looks like it has a job to do.
explanation.definitionFit: An EVADER is somebody who ducks a duty, a question or the taxman, so the plural matches 'People who dodge'.

clue.text: Twit canoodles with action film director

indicators.note: Something done with action is in motion, and letters in motion do not stay in the order they were printed.

parts.note: thirteen letters of fodder, splitting 5 and 8 as the enumeration asks

explanation.surface: A fool having a cuddle in the middle of an action picture.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is a complete little sentence in itself, which is the disguise — nothing in 'Twit canoodles' reads as an instruction, so the eye slides past to the film.
explanation.definitionFit: Clint Eastwood directed Unforgiven and Million Dollar Baby among many more, so 'film director' names the job behind the acting fame.

clue.text: Give out porridge on return

indicators.note: Coming back means retracing the way you came, so the letters are read from their far end backwards.

parts.note: doing porridge is British slang for serving a prison sentence, so porridge is time

explanation.surface: Handing round the breakfast when somebody comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: Porridge for a prison stretch is British prison slang old enough to have named a sitcom, and it is one of the words a setter uses whenever a clue needs four ordinary letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To EMIT light, heat or a smell is to send it out from yourself, which is what 'give out' means as a verb.

clue.text: Fulmar gets confused in current across the pond

indicators.note: Something confused has lost track of what goes where, so the letters beside the word do not keep the arrangement they arrived in.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, which is what the 4,6 enumeration asks for

explanation.surface: A seabird getting itself thoroughly muddled out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: A fulmar is a stiff-winged North Atlantic seabird, so bird and definition share an ocean, and 'the pond' is the British nickname for that same Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: The GULF STREAM is the warm current running from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic to Europe, and 'the pond' is that ocean.

clue.text: Earnest camping like this?

indicators.note: The question points at the letters in front of you: split them into two words and they describe the state named just before.

parts.note: a camper spends the night inside something, and the two-letter word for inside comes first
the canvas that camper is sleeping under supplies the other four letters

explanation.surface: A serious-minded camping trip, done in exactly this fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one word the answer is a state of mind; read as two it is where a camper sleeps, and the question mark is the setter admitting the join.
explanation.definitionFit: INTENT as an adjective means fixed earnestly on something — an intent stare, intent on winning — which is the sense 'Earnest' carries.

clue.text: Celebrities can't play snooker for this reason

parts.note: the flat two-letter refusal that explains why something cannot happen
snooker is played on big baize-covered tables, so the game hands over its own equipment

explanation.surface: A room full of famous people who cannot get a game of snooker.
explanation.walkthrough: The reason really is spelled out: say the eight letters as two words and you have the shortage that stops the game, which is why 'for this reason' is a promise rather than padding.
explanation.definitionFit: NOTABLES are the people worth noting — the distinguished names on a guest list — which is what 'Celebrities' means.

clue.text: Map a creek for training frontrunner

indicators.note: Training a squad knocks it into a different shape, so the letters put through it do not come out standing where they started.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, with the two A's and two E's easy to lose count of

explanation.surface: Charting a small tidal inlet as part of somebody's training.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frontrunner' looks like one more piece of the training story, which is the whole disguise — a map and a creek belong to an exercise, not to a race.
explanation.definitionFit: A PACEMAKER is the runner who leads a race and sets the speed for the field, so the definition names that position.

clue.text: Superficially less cross, for ever

indicators.note: Less works as minus here, so whatever is named after it comes away from the letters you already have.

parts.note: what is superficial is on the outside only, and the adverb for that is the ten letters to start from
a cross is written as the letter X, as on a ballot paper or the end of a note

explanation.surface: Somebody only slightly less bad-tempered, and staying that way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' reads as the mood in the sentence and is the shape of a letter in the wordplay, which is one of the standard ways a setter clues X.
explanation.definitionFit: ETERNALLY means going on without any end, which is what 'for ever' says in two words.

clue.text: German defeat provides sheen

parts.note: g is the standard abbreviation for the language and the nationality
a match you did not win goes down as a loss

explanation.surface: A German setback that turns out to have a bright side.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves read as a single idea, a German defeat, so the join between the one-letter piece and the four-letter one leaves no seam to see.
explanation.definitionFit: GLOSS is the shine on a polished surface — gloss paint, a glossy magazine — so 'sheen' is a plain synonym for the noun.

clue.text: Some males sexualised in part of eastern England

indicators.note: Some of a phrase is a piece of it taken as it stands, so a run of letters is wanted rather than the words themselves.

parts.note: five letters in a row, beginning inside the first word and finishing inside the second

explanation.surface: An observation about the way some men get sexualised.
explanation.walkthrough: A buried answer hides best inside a phrase that reads as ordinary comment, and this one sounds like a line from a newspaper column rather than a set of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: ESSEX is the county on the North Sea coast immediately east of London, so the definition places it geographically.

clue.text: High pitched squawk rocks church

parts.note: scree is the loose broken rock that piles up down a mountainside
ch is the standard abbreviation, the one printed on maps

explanation.surface: A noise loud enough to shake a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' reads as a verb, the noise shaking the building, and is a plain noun in the wordplay — the loose stuff lying on a hillside.
explanation.definitionFit: A SCREECH is a harsh high-pitched cry, the noise an owl or a set of brakes makes, which is the squawk described.

clue.text: When I am wearing gold in part of Turkey

parts.note: as and when open a clause interchangeably
the two words used exactly as printed
somebody wearing black is in black, so the word stands in for the little preposition
or is the heraldic word for gold, the metal on a coat of arms

explanation.surface: Somebody describing themselves turned out in gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing' looks like the container instruction this clue never uses; it is a piece in its own right, standing in for a two-letter preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: ASIA MINOR is the old name for the Anatolian peninsula, which makes up the great bulk of modern Turkey.

clue.text: So be it: sex with unknown for convenience

parts.note: the word said at the close of a prayer means precisely that
it is the coy old word for sex, as in the 1920s It girl who had sex appeal
x, y and z are the letters algebra keeps for quantities not yet known

explanation.surface: A shrug of agreement to a fling with a stranger.
explanation.walkthrough: Three scraps of shorthand stacked up, and the one to keep is the algebra: any of x, y or z can be an unknown, so the crossing letters decide which one is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: An AMENITY is a facility that makes life easier — a park bench, a laundry room — which is what a convenience is, public ones included.

clue.text: Go on too long in swamp

definitions.meaning: what a meeting or a speech does when it eats into the next slot
the verb, meaning to flood a place or overwhelm somebody with more than they can take

explanation.surface: A meeting dragging on somewhere marshy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swamp' is the trap: it reads as the noun, a patch of wet ground, and the clue wants the verb, to overwhelm by sheer numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A talk that OVERRUNS goes past its allotted time, and to OVERRUN a country or a system is to swamp it with more than it can hold.

clue.text: Seizes power in shop

indicators.note: The piece named before it goes inside the word named after it, rather than being written alongside.

parts.note: to shop somebody is to inform on them, and grass is the same British slang for doing it
p is the standard abbreviation in physics

explanation.surface: A power grab in a corner shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shop' is not the place you buy things but the verb, to inform on somebody — the same idea as grassing on them, which is why the two words swap so neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: To GRASP something is to take firm hold of it, so 'Seizes' matches both the sense and the third-person ending.

clue.text: Some rugby players argue with impudence, at first

indicators.note: This fixes a position rather than picking out a letter: the piece just named goes at the start of the answer.

parts.note: front is cheek or nerve — 'what a front!' — said of somebody brazen
a row is a noisy quarrel, the one that rhymes with cow

explanation.surface: Rugby forwards squaring up and giving lip before anything else happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like an instruction to take initial letters and is only saying which piece leads. A front row is the two props and the hooker who bind at the head of a rugby scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: The FRONT ROW is that trio of forwards at the head of the scrum, so the definition names them as one group within a rugby team.

clue.text: Student has left out source of money

indicators.note: Out marks a removal: the letter named just before it is taken out of the longer word it sits in.

parts.note: a student is a learner, and those seven letters are what you start from
l is the standard abbreviation, the one on a pair of gloves

explanation.surface: A student who has walked out on a steady income.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has left' reads as departed, and that hides both halves of the instruction at once: 'left' names the letter and 'out' says what becomes of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An EARNER is a thing that brings money in — 'a nice little earner' — so it is a source of money rather than the person paid.

clue.text: Dance in strange bar, mostly

indicators.note: Most of a word is all of it bar the last letter, so the tail is dropped before the piece is used.

parts.note: rum is an old British adjective for odd or peculiar — 'a rum do'
the three-letter word with its tail taken off

explanation.surface: A dance held in a decidedly odd little bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' for strange is Victorian slang that survives almost nowhere but crosswords, and it slides into a sentence about a bar without a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The RUMBA is the Cuban ballroom dance, so 'Dance' defines it by naming the class it belongs to.

clue.text: Rub close-in when partying — this PM liked to

indicators.note: A party is where order breaks down and everybody ends up somewhere they did not start, and so do these letters.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the hyphen ignored as hyphens always are
surface only: it ties the picture to the man and hands over no letters

explanation.surface: A politician with a taste for getting far too close to people at parties.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bunga bunga' parties were front-page news across Europe for years, which is what lets the fodder read as biography instead of as a bag of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Silvio Berlusconi was Italy's prime minister four separate times, so 'this PM' points at one particular holder of that office.

clue.text: Unpleasant situation of male anger

parts.note: m is the standard abbreviation, the box you tick on a form
ire is the poetic word for anger, three letters setters lean on constantly

explanation.surface: One man's temper making everything worse.
explanation.walkthrough: A MIRE is literally a bog, and it is the figurative sense the definition wants — stuck fast in something you cannot get yourself out of.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in a MIRE is to be bogged down in a mess with no easy way out, which is an unpleasant situation.

clue.text: Why is husband claiming base is like dairy product?

indicators.note: To claim something is to take it in and keep hold of it, so the letter named is swallowed inside the word doing the claiming.

parts.note: the question word spelled out, three letters waiting to be opened up
e is the base of natural logarithms in mathematics
the little verb used exactly as printed
h is the standard abbreviation, the one on a family tree

explanation.surface: A husband staking a claim to the base, and somebody demanding to know why.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' is the mathematician's e, the number at the bottom of natural logarithms, and it is the kind of one-letter convention worth keeping for good.
explanation.definitionFit: WHEYISH means resembling whey, the thin liquid left when milk curdles for cheese, so the definition points at that dairy product.

clue.text: Absolute power of extremely tetchy grandma not good

indicators.note: Extremely sends you to both far ends of the word it marks, so the first and last letters are all you keep.
Not marks an absence: whatever is named after it is missing from the letters you have just been given.

parts.note: the two letters at the outer edges of the word, taken at its extremes
granny is the everyday word for a grandmother
g is the standard abbreviation, as in a grade on a school report

explanation.surface: A short-tempered grandmother behaving at her absolute worst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not good' reads as a verdict on the old lady and is really a pair of instructions: the abbreviation for good, and the word that takes it away again.
explanation.definitionFit: TYRANNY is rule by someone whose power has no check on it at all, which is what 'Absolute power' describes.
